metadata.title: GNRK: Graph Neural Runge-Kutta method for solving partial differential equations

section.title: Introduction
section.summary: The introduction motivates neural network-based PDE solvers and contrasts them with classical solvers in terms of efficiency, versatility, and robustness to changing PDE conditions. It introduces Graph Neural Runge-Kutta as a hybrid of Runge-Kutta numerical integration and graph neural networks, intended for PDEs and coupled differential equations on Euclidean or graph domains.

item.text: NN-based PDE solvers may perform poorly or be inapplicable when initial conditions, PDE coefficients, or spatiotemporal meshes differ from training conditions.
Classical solvers handle varied PDE forms and conditions given the exact PDE, while NN solvers can be efficient surrogate models.
GNRK reconstructs the RK method as a recurrent structure with residual connections and approximates the governing function using a GNN.
The method is claimed to be independent of spatial and temporal discretization and robust to changes in initial conditions and PDE coefficients.
The authors state that prediction accuracy can be controlled by adjusting RK order through recurrent depth.
The paper claims GNRK can solve PDEs regardless of initial conditions, PDE coefficients, and spatiotemporal mesh, and can improve precision without retraining.

section.title: Graph Neural Runge-Kutta
section.summary: This section formulates the PDE setting, describes temporal and spatial discretization as graph structures, reviews the explicit Runge-Kutta update, and defines the GNRK architecture. The model uses a shared GNN module inside a recurrent RK-like structure and is trained with one-step MSE loss, then rolled out over trajectories.

item.text: The target dynamics are written as ∂s(x,t)/∂t = f(s; C), with coefficients C and spatial domain Ω.
Spatial discretizations, including nonuniform Euclidean grids and graph domains, are represented as graphs whose node updates use neighboring states.
The explicit RK update uses intermediate values and Butcher tableau coefficients to compute s(x_i,t+Δt).
GNRK reproduces RK^m as a recurrent structure of depth m with residual connections, sharing f_θ across substeps.
The GNN uses node, edge, and global features, MLP encoders, graph network modules, aggregation, and an MLP decoder.
Training minimizes one-step Mean Squared Error between s(t+Δt) and the predicted next state.

section.title: Generalization Capability
section.summary: This section categorizes generalization criteria into initial conditions, PDE coefficients, spatial discretization, and temporal discretization with RK order. It explains how the GNRK design is intended to handle each criterion through localized graph computations, feature-encoded coefficients, graph representations of grids, and RK recurrence controlled by Δt and order m.

item.text: Localized GNN computations are presented as the reason GNRK can learn transitions across varied initial conditions using few samples.
PDE coefficients are categorized as node, edge, or global coefficients and can be provided as GNN input features.
For Euclidean domains, GNRK can encode coordinates as node features or relative positions as edge features to operate on nonuniform grids.
For graph domains, GNRK is described as applicable to changing connectivity structures and different numbers of nodes and edges.
Temporal step sizes and RK order are handled in the recurrent structure, allowing predictions with unseen Δt and modified m without retraining.
The authors state that changing m can be useful when training data have lower numerical precision than deployment requirements.

section.title: Experiment: Euclidean Spatial Domain
section.summary: This section evaluates GNRK on the 2D Burgers' equation over a periodic square domain. Four datasets vary initial conditions, viscosity, spatial discretization, and temporal discretization/RK precision, and results are compared against PINN, FNO, GNO, and GraphPDE using MAE, parameter count, wall-clock time, and GPU memory.

item.text: 2D Burgers' equation on Ω=[0,1]^2 and T=[0,1] with periodic boundary condition and viscosity ν.
Datasets I-IV vary initial conditions, viscosity coefficient ν, nonuniform grid size, and nonuniform temporal steps with training RK1 and test RK4.
Baselines include PINN, FNO, GNO, and GraphPDE; FNO and GNO use 100 training samples for reported comparisons.
Predictive performance is quantified by mean absolute error averaged over nodes and the u and v states.
GNRK MAEs are reported as 1.04e-3, 1.13e-3, 4.56e-3, and 1.44e-3 on Datasets I-IV, respectively.
GNRK is reported with 10,882 trainable parameters, 7.32±0.10 s wall-clock time, and 153 MiB GPU memory.

section.title: Experiment: Graph Spatial Domain
section.summary: This section applies GNRK to three coupled ODE systems on graph spatial domains: heat diffusion, Kuramoto oscillators, and coupled Rössler attractors. The datasets vary initial conditions, coefficients, graph sizes, graph topology, temporal discretization, and RK precision, and evaluate prediction errors and topology effects.

item.text: Graph heat equation models node temperatures with edge dissipation rates D_ij.
Kuramoto equation models oscillator phase θ_i using node angular velocity ω_i and edge coupling K_ij.
Coupled Rössler equation models graph-coupled chaotic attractors with global coefficients a, b, c and edge coupling K_ij.
Precision comparison evaluates predictions using RK1 versus RK4, with RK1 used in training and RK4 used for higher-precision testing.
Topology comparison reports MAE for random regular, Erdős-Rényi, and Barabási-Albert graphs.
The reported MAE with RK1 is about 10 times larger than after tuning GNRK to RK4 for the graph-domain systems.

section.title: Conclusion and Appendices
section.summary: The conclusion summarizes GNRK as a hybrid neural PDE solver using RK recurrence and GNN modules, emphasizing robustness to initial conditions, coefficients, discretization, and adjustable precision. The appendices provide nonuniform-grid derivative formulas and detailed dataset, model, and optimization configurations for Burgers' and coupled ODE experiments.

item.text: GNRK is summarized as able to predict solutions under different initial conditions and PDE coefficients and to be invariant to spatial and temporal discretization.
Nonuniform square-grid differentiation follows the Sundqvist and Veronis method for first and second derivatives.
Burgers' grid-to-graph transformation encodes relative edge distances and directions as edge features.
Coupled ODE experiments use graph sizes from 50 to 150 nodes, mean degrees from 2 to 6, RR/ER/BA topologies, nonuniform time steps, RK1 training, and RK4 evaluation.
The conclusion lists further enhancement avenues including adaptive spatiotemporal discretization using intermediate results.
The conclusion lists addressing equations from noisy partial observations as a future enhancement.

claims.item: GNRK combines an RK recurrent structure with a GNN approximation of the governing function.
The method is claimed to handle changes in initial conditions, PDE coefficients, and spatiotemporal meshes.
The authors claim prediction accuracy can be controlled by changing RK order through recurrent depth.
The paper claims GNRK can generalize to varied initial conditions, coefficients, spatial discretizations, temporal discretizations, and graph topologies without retraining.
The conclusion claims precision can exceed that of training data by modifying RK order without additional training.

method_components.item: Explicit Runge-Kutta update represented as a recurrent neural structure with residual connections.
Shared GNN module f_θ approximates the governing differential equation f.
GNN inputs include node, edge, and global features, each embedded by MLP encoders.
Graph network module updates edge features, aggregates messages, updates node features, and decodes W.
Training uses one-step MSE and rollout prediction for full trajectories.
Nonuniform-grid numerical differentiation is used for Burgers' data generation.

datasets.item: 2D Burgers' equation on a periodic square domain with coupled u and v velocity fields.
Dataset I varies initial phases and offsets of asymmetric sine initial conditions.
Dataset II varies viscosity ν from 0.005 to 0.02.
Dataset III varies nonuniform grid sizes from 50 to 150 along each axis.
Dataset IV varies nonuniform temporal discretization and uses RK1 training data with RK4 test data.
Graph-domain datasets include heat, Kuramoto, and coupled Rössler systems on RR, ER, and BA graphs.

baselines.item: PINN is used as an equation-based baseline where applicable.
FNO is used as a neural operator baseline on compatible uniform-grid/fixed-time settings.
GNO is used as a graph neural operator baseline where applicable.
GraphPDE is used as a graph-based baseline applicable to all four Burgers' datasets.
A classical numerical solver wall-clock time is reported for reference.

ablations.item: RK1 versus RK4 precision comparison in graph-domain experiments.
Topology comparison across RR, ER, and BA graphs.
Dataset IV tests temporal discretization and train/test RK-order difference.

metrics.item: One-step training loss is Mean Squared Error.
Evaluation metric for Burgers' trajectories is Mean Absolute Error averaged over nodes and states.
Table 1 reports MAE, trainable parameter count, wall-clock time, and GPU memory.
Graph-domain experiments report Mean Absolute Error on logarithmic scale.

results.item: GNRK reports MAE 1.04e-3 on Burgers' Dataset I.
GNRK reports MAE 1.13e-3 on Burgers' Dataset II.
GNRK reports MAE 4.56e-3 on Burgers' Dataset III.
GNRK reports MAE 1.44e-3 on Burgers' Dataset IV.
GNRK is reported with 10,882 parameters, fewer than the listed baselines in Table 1.
For graph-domain systems, RK1 prediction errors are reported as about 10 times larger than RK4-tuned prediction errors.
The authors report no significant performance differences based on RR, ER, or BA topology.

stated_limitations.item: Adaptive spatiotemporal discretization using intermediate results is listed as a possible future enhancement.
Solving equations from noisy partial observations is listed as a future challenge.
